From @Shelly38499228: as Digit moves toward broader deployment, which mechanical parts changed the most between versions, and which did you deliberately freeze to make production and service easier?

Nearly every part changed between Digit 4 and Digit 5. Digit 4 was the first commercially deployed humanoid robot, and with that time in the field, we learned so much about customer requirements. We were able to do a full, formal product design process, involving hundreds of customer requirements that translated into hundreds of engineering requirements. We retained many features and engineering solutions, but the components are nearly all different and updated. Many include new design-for-manufacture, such as sheet metal, casting, or other high-volume manufacturing processes. Digit 5 will be easier to build and easier to service because of engineering changes made based on learnings from Digit 4.

From @Chama1176: I love Cassie. What were the trade-offs involved in transitioning from leaf springs (in Digit 3) to rigid links (incorporating torque or force sensing?) in Digit 4?

Leaf springs are great for handling harsh impacts during a running gait, but they add complex dynamics (and of course mechanical complexity) when you’re trying to stand and manipulate things. Cassie was optimized for walking and running; Digit is optimized for locomanipulation. And now with Digit 5, the human-style leg configuration is designed so the robot will have the ability to lift heavy things while getting low to the ground.

From @RoboPromoEvents: what was the hardest part of getting Digit to move so naturally around people? Big fans of the work.

JH: The hardest part is priorities: We know how to do the dynamics and how to create beautiful, natural gaits. And it’s especially straightforward with a smaller, lighter robot, like Cassie. Now, with Digit 5 at over 120kgs, it requires special actuators and leg configurations to get the power and strength at the same time as the natural dynamic motion. In addition, the team is so focused on customer use cases, improving manipulation capabilities, reliability, active deployments, safety, and more, that dialing in the gait dynamics just isn’t a priority and won’t be the thing keeping Digit 5 from doing its job well. This is part of why Agility and Digit 5 are special - we are focused on solving customer applications, not just doing demonstrations, and achieving dynamic locomotion will be part of that focus. 

The hardest part around people was safety, and what I learned is that predictability matters more than grace. A coworker needs to know what the robot will do next. So Digit 5 is designed to  detect people, react in real time and move predictably, with lights and sounds that signal its intent. That took us two years, and I still want it to move beautifully.
